text: A log line that reads perfectly well to you in a terminal can still be a dead end at production scale. The moment you have thousands of instances writing millions of lines a day, and you need a precise answer across all of them, free text turns into a fragile regular expression that breaks the next time someone reworks the wording. This lesson is about making a log line something a machine can query, not just something a human can skim.

Here's that classic line: an error, an order number, a user, a timeout, all woven into a sentence. Readable, sure. But ask for every failed order in the EU in the last hour, grouped by failure reason, and you're guessing at where the order number and the region sit in the sentence — pattern-matching prose instead of querying data.

Structured logging means every line is emitted as a well-defined data structure, almost always JSON, with named fields instead of a freeform sentence. Same facts as before — timestamp, level, service, the order ID, the region, the duration, the error — but now every one of them lives at a known address. A log backend can index order_id and region as real fields and run exactly the query you wanted, with no regex and no breakage when the wording changes.

A few fields earn their place in nearly every log line because they're what make individual lines joinable into a bigger story. Timestamp, level, and service tell you when, how severe, and who. The event field is a stable, machine-friendly name for what happened, independent of any human prose. And trace_id is the hinge between pillars — it's what lets you jump from a slow span in a trace straight to the exact log lines that request produced.

A log level isn't decoration, it's what downstream tooling filters and alerts on. ERROR means this operation failed and probably needs attention. WARN means something unexpected happened but the request still completed. INFO is a normal, expected lifecycle event worth keeping. DEBUG is detail you only want while actively troubleshooting, and it's usually sampled or dropped before it ever leaves the host — because storing every debug line forever is the fastest way to make your logging bill bigger than your compute bill.

Structure the line, carry a trace_id through it, and pick the level on purpose — that's what turns a log from something you read into something you query. Next lesson picks up that trace_id directly: how a trace actually gets created and propagated across service boundaries.
